llm.summary: The skill mostly matches its cat-status purpose, but it can send your LLM API key and prompt data to any configured API endpoint without validation or a clear warning.

dimensions.detail: The implementation accepts 'base_url' from config and sends the API key plus system/user prompt content to that URL for every supported provider without validating scheme, host, or provider match. This is broader than needed for the documented official providers and could expose credentials if a user or attacker supplies an untrusted endpoint.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: Installation asks users to run an unpinned 'pip install requests' and create a local config containing an API key. This is common for a Python integration, but it is not reproducible and lacks stronger secret-handling guidance.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Activation is broader than a strict /cat command because the docs also allow natural-language cat-check requests, but the examples remain tied to the stated cat-status purpose. The roleplay prompt's 'always answer as the cat' wording appears scoped to character consistency, not a general anti-refusal override.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The only code-created persistent state observed is '.cat_cache.json' in the skill directory, storing randomly generated cat attributes. It is disclosed in the docs and is low sensitivity, though there is no disable or clear-cache control.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The core behavior is coherent: it generates a cat persona, builds prompts, and calls a selected LLM provider to answer as the cat. I did not find unrelated command execution, broad file reads, destructive behavior, or hidden background work.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Review this skill before installing. Use only trusted provider endpoints, leave custom base_url empty unless you understand that the endpoint will receive your API key and prompt data, and prefer scoped or low-quota API keys. Expect a local cat-profile cache file to be created.
llm.findings:
[T09] unexpected: Accepted as a material Review concern: custom endpoints are optional, but the code forwards credential-bearing headers and prompt data to unvalidated configured destinations.
[T08] expected: The unpinned 'requests' install is a low-level supply-chain hygiene issue, not evidence of malicious packaging or unsafe package sources.
[E1] expected: Outbound LLM calls are expected for this skill, but the combination of prompt transmission, API keys, and arbitrary base_url makes the data flow under-scoped.
[SQP-2] expected: Remote prompt transmission and local cache persistence are part of the design, but the user-facing docs do not clearly explain that provider APIs or custom endpoints receive prompt/profile data and credentials.
[LP3] unexpected: The skill does not declare explicit permission boundaries for network, config, or cache access. This is not malicious by itself, but it compounds the custom-endpoint concern.
[SQP-1] expected: Natural-language triggers such as 'Check on my cat' are broader than command-only activation but remain aligned with the documented use case.
[SQP-3] expected: The mixed Chinese implementation text and English response instruction are usability/localization issues, not security-significant privilege or data-flow concerns.
[P6] expected: Downgraded: the flagged 'return prompt' is a helper returning the constructed user prompt for the provider call, not an instruction to reveal hidden system prompts.
[AR1] expected: Downgraded: 'Always answer as the cat' is part of the roleplay format and does not appear to override general platform safety rules.
